DIV{HEADER1{minimalPresentationMapInv,  -- compute a minimal presentation of a quotient ring}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{S = minimalPresentation R, class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{S = prune R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{R}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Ring, ring}}, , , a quotient ring}}}}, LI{TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: using functions with optional inputs, Optional inputs}, :, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{Exclude}, TT{ => }, TT{...}, , , SPAN{default value , {}}}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{S}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Ring, ring}}, , , a quotient ring, minimally presented if , TT{R},  is homogeneous, isomorphic to , TT{R}}}}}, LI{DIV{Consequences:, UL{LI{the isomorphism from , TT{R},  to , TT{S},  is stored as , TT{R.minimalPresentationMap},  and the inverse of this map is stored as , TT{R.minimalPresentationMapInv}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, The computation is accomplished by considering the relations of , TT{R}, . If a variable occurs as a term of a relation of , TT{R},  and in no other terms of the same polynomial, then  the variable is replaced by the remaining terms and removed from the ring.  A minimal generating set for the resulting defining ideal is then computed and the new quotient ring is returned. If , TT{R},  is not homogeneous, then an attempt is made to improve the presentation., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = ZZ/101[x,y,z,u,w]/ideal(x-x^2-y,z+x*y,w^2-u^2);, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : minimalPresentation(R)

      ZZ
     ---[x, u, w]
     101
o2 = ------------
          2    2
       - u  + w

o2 : QuotientRing, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : R.minimalPresentationMap

           ZZ
          ---[x, u, w]
          101                     2       3    2
o3 = map (------------, R, {x, - x  + x, x  - x , u, w})
               2    2
            - u  + w

              ZZ
             ---[x, u, w]
             101
o3 : RingMap ------------ <-- R
                  2    2
               - u  + w, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : R.minimalPresentationMapInv

              ZZ
             ---[x, u, w]
             101
o4 = map (R, ------------, {x, u, w})
                  2    2
               - u  + w

                    ZZ
                   ---[x, u, w]
                   101
o4 : RingMap R <-- ------------
                        2    2
                     - u  + w, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, If the Exclude option is present, then those variables with the given indices are not simplified away (remember that ring variable indices start at 0)., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : R = ZZ/101[x,y,z,u,w]/ideal(x-x^2-y,z+x*y,w^2-u^2);, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : minimalPresentation(R, Exclude=>{1})

           ZZ
          ---[x..y, u, w]
          101
o6 = -------------------------
         2             2    2
     (- x  + x - y, - u  + w )

o6 : QuotientRing, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: minimalPresentation(Ideal)}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: prune(Ideal)}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: trim(Ring)}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: trim(QuotientRing)}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: minimalPresentationMapInv},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Symbol, symbol}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/functions/minimalPresentation-doc.m2:54:0}, .}}}}

An option of the form }, TT{"name" => "symbol"}, TEX{ creates a symbol with the name }, TT{name}, TEX{ that is a synonym of the symbol }, TT{symbol}, TEX{.}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, DIV{PARA{TEX{A package can contain the code for many functions, only some of which should be made visible to the user. full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{MonomialOrder,  -- monomial ordering}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, TT{MonomialOrder},  -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic)., PARA{}, In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations., PARA{}, In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of , EM{ordering tests}, , of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: monomial orderings}, ., PARA{}, Permissible elements:, UL{LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GRevLex},  => n -- A graded reverse lexicographic block of variables}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Lex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Weights},  => {...}}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Position},  => Up  or  Position => Down}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: RevLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GroupLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GroupRevLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MonomialSize},  => n, n being 8,16,32, or 64.  Set the packing size for exponents for further variables}}, PARA{}, Some examples of monomial orders.  Note that if only one item is in the list, we can dispense with the list., UL{LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {GRevLex=>2, GRevLex=>3}},  -- a product order}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {2, 3}},  -- same}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {Weights=>{1,13,6,2}}},  -- a weight order}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => Weights=>{1,13,6,2}},  -- same}}, If any monomials will be less than 1 in the ordering, then the option , TT{Global => false},  should be used., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : QQ[x,y, Weights => {-1,1}, Global => false]

o1 = QQ[x..y]

name: RR
full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{RR,  -- the class of all real numbers}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, A real number is entered as a sequence of decimal digits with a point.  It is stored internally as an arbitrary precision floating point number, using the , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MPFR},  library., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : 3.14159

o1 = 3.14159

o1 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The precision is measured in bits, is visible in the ring displayed on the second of each pair of output lines, and can be recovered using , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: precision}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : precision 3.14159

o2 = 53, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, For real numbers, the functions , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: class},  and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ring},  yield different results.  That allows numbers of various precisions to be used without creating a new ring for each precision., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : class 3.1

o3 = RR

o3 : InexactFieldFamily, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : ring 3.1

o4 = RR
       53

o4 : RealField, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The precision can be specified on input by appending the letter , TT{p},  and a positive number., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : 3p300

o5 = 3

o5 : RR (of precision 300), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, An optional exponent (for the power of ten to multiply by) can be specified on input by appending the letter , TT{e},  and a number., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : 3e3

o6 = 3000

o6 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : -3e-3

o8 = -.003

o8 : RR (of precision 111), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Numbers that appear alone on an output line are displayed with all their meaningful digits. (Specifying 100 bits of precision yields about 30 decimal digits of precision.), TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : 1/3.

o9 = .3333333333333333

o9 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : 1/3p100

o14 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i15 : .2p100 == .2p30

o15 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The notion of (strict) equality tested by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ===},  also takes the precision into account., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i16 : .5p100 === .5p30

name: combine
full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{combine,  -- combine hash tables}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{z = combine(x,y,f,g,h) or z=combine(x,y,f,t,g,h), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{x}, , , a hash table}}, LI{SPAN{TT{y}, , , a hash table of the same class as , TT{x}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{f}, , , a function of two variables to be used for combining a key of , TT{x},  with a key of , TT{y},  to make a new key for , TT{z}, .}}, LI{SPAN{TT{t}, , , a function combining two keys and returning a value, twisting the value returned by , TT{g},  based on which keys were used. This argument may be omitted, in which case the , TT{t(p,q)},  term in the output below is omitted.}}, LI{SPAN{TT{g}, , , a function of two variables to be used for combining a value of , TT{x},  with a value of , TT{y},  to make a new value for , TT{z}, .}}, LI{SPAN{TT{h}, , , a function of two variables to be used for combining two values returned by , TT{g},  when the corresponding keys returned by , TT{f},  turn out to be equal.  Its first argument will be the value accumulated so far, and its second argument will be a value just provided by , TT{g}, .}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{z}, , , a new hash table, of the same class as , TT{x},  and , TT{y}, , containing the pair , TT{f(p,q) => g(t(p,q),g(b,c))},  whenever , TT{x},  contains the pair , TT{p => b},  and , TT{y},  contains the pair , TT{q => c}, , except that , TT{h},  is used to combine values when two keys coincide.  If , TT{f},  or , TT{g},  evaluates , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: continue}, , then nothing is contributed to the resulting hash table.  If , TT{h},  evaluates , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: continue}, , then, at that point, the entry stored under the key , TT{f(p,q)},  in the hash table under construction is removed.}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, The function , TT{f},  is applied to every pair , TT{(p,q)},  where , TT{p},  is a key of , TT{x},  and , TT{q},  is a key of , TT{y}, .  The number of times , TT{f},  is evaluated is thus the product of the number of keys in , TT{x},  and the number of keys in , TT{y}, ., PARA{}, The function , TT{h},  should be an associative function, for otherwise the result may depend on internal details about the implementation of hash tables that affect the order in which entries are encountered.  If , TT{f}, , , TT{t},  (if present), , TT{g}, , and , TT{h},  are commutative functions as well, then the result , TT{z},  is a commutative function of , TT{x},  and , TT{y}, ., PARA{}, The result is mutable if and only if , TT{x},  or , TT{y},  is., PARA{}, This function can be used for multiplying polynomials, where it can be used in code something like this:, PRE{     combine(x, y, monomialTimes, coeffTimes, coeffPlus)}, We illustrate that with a simple-minded implementation of the free ring on the English alphabet, representing words as string and polynomials as hash tables that associate coefficients to words., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : Poly = new Type of HashTable

o1 = Poly

o1 : Type, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : p = new Poly from { "" => 1, "x" => 2, "y" => 3, "cat" => 5 }

o2 = Poly{"" => 1   }
          "cat" => 5
          "x" => 2
          "y" => 3

o2 : Poly, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : Poly * Poly := (p,q) -> combine(p,q,concatenate,times,plus);, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : p*p

o4 = Poly{"" => 1       }
          "cat" => 10
          "catcat" => 25
          "catx" => 10
          "caty" => 15
          "x" => 4
          "xcat" => 10
          "xx" => 4
          "xy" => 6
          "y" => 6
          "ycat" => 15
          "yx" => 6
          "yy" => 9

o4 : Poly, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, One may also use this function for multiplying divided powers in a similar manner:, PRE{     combine(x, y, monomialTimes, divPowCoeff, coeffTimes, coeffPlus)}, For example:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : DivPowPoly = new Type of HashTable

o5 = DivPowPoly

o5 : Type, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : divPowCoeff = (i,j) -> binomial(i+j,i)

o6 = divPowCoeff

o6 : FunctionClosure, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : p = new DivPowPoly from { 0 => 1, 1 => 1 }

o7 = DivPowPoly{0 => 1}
                1 => 1

o7 : DivPowPoly, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : DivPowPoly * DivPowPoly := (p,q) -> combine(p,q,plus,divPowCoeff,times,plus);, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : p*p

o9 = DivPowPoly{0 => 1}
                1 => 2
                2 => 2

o9 : DivPowPoly, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: merge}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: combine},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: CompiledFunction, compiled function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/functions/combine-doc.m2:75:0}, .}}}}

full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{Up,  -- monomial ordering}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, TT{MonomialOrder},  -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic)., PARA{}, In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations., PARA{}, In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of , EM{ordering tests}, , of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: monomial orderings}, ., PARA{}, Permissible elements:, UL{LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GRevLex},  => n -- A graded reverse lexicographic block of variables}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Lex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Weights},  => {...}}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Position},  => Up  or  Position => Down}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: RevLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GroupLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GroupRevLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MonomialSize},  => n, n being 8,16,32, or 64.  Set the packing size for exponents for further variables}}, PARA{}, Some examples of monomial orders.  Note that if only one item is in the list, we can dispense with the list., UL{LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {GRevLex=>2, GRevLex=>3}},  -- a product order}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {2, 3}},  -- same}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {Weights=>{1,13,6,2}}},  -- a weight order}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => Weights=>{1,13,6,2}},  -- same}}, If any monomials will be less than 1 in the ordering, then the option , TT{Global => false},  should be used., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : QQ[x,y, Weights => {-1,1}, Global => false]

o1 = QQ[x..y]

name: memoize
full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{memoize,  -- record results of function evaluation for future use}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, TT{memoize f},  -- produces, from a function , TT{f}, , a new function that behaves the same as , TT{f}, , but remembers previous answers to be provided the next time the same arguments are presented., PARA{}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : fib = n -> if n <= 1 then 1 else fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)

o1 = fib

o1 : FunctionClosure, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : time fib 28
 -- used 0.54804s (cpu); 0.429224s (thread); 0s (gc)

o2 = 514229, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : fib = memoize fib

o3 = fib

o3 : FunctionClosure, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : time fib 28
 -- used 5.535e-05s (cpu); 5.5032e-05s (thread); 0s (gc)

o4 = 514229, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : time fib 28
 -- used 1.659e-06s (cpu); 1.562e-06s (thread); 0s (gc)

o5 = 514229, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{An optional second argument to memoize provides a list of initial values, each of the form , TT{x => v}, , where , TT{v},  is the value to be provided for the argument , TT{x}, .}, PARA{Alternatively, values can be provided after defining the memoized function using the syntax , TT{f x = v}, . A slightly more efficient implementation of the above would be}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : fib = memoize( n -> fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) )

o6 = fib

o6 : FunctionClosure, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : fib 0 = fib 1 = 1;, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : fib 28

o8 = 514229, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{The function , TT{memoize},  operates by constructing a , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MutableHashTable}, , in which the arguments are used as keys for accessing the return value of the function.  This mutable hash table can be obtained using the function , TT{memoizeValues}, , as follows.}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : peek memoizeValues fib

o9 = MutableHashTable{0 => 1      }
                      1 => 1
                      2 => 2
                      3 => 3
                      4 => 5
                      5 => 8
                      6 => 13
                      7 => 21
                      8 => 34
                      9 => 55
                      10 => 89
                      11 => 144
                      12 => 233
                      13 => 377
                      14 => 610
                      15 => 987
                      16 => 1597
                      17 => 2584
                      18 => 4181
                      19 => 6765
                      20 => 10946
                      21 => 17711
                      22 => 28657
                      23 => 46368
                      24 => 75025
                      25 => 121393
                      26 => 196418
                      27 => 317811
                      28 => 514229, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{That hash table can be replaced by an empty one with the function , TT{memoizeClear}, .}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : memoizeClear fib, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : peek memoizeValues fib

o11 = MutableHashTable{}, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{Warning: the new function created by , TT{memoize},  will save references to all arguments and values it encounters, and this will often prevent those arguments and values from being garbage-collected as soon as they might have been.  If the arguments are implemented as mutable hash tables (modules, matrices and rings are implemented this way) then a viable strategy is to stash computed results in the arguments themselves.  See also , TT{CacheTable}, .}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{memoize}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{memoize(Function)}}, LI{KBD{memoize(Function,List)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: memoize},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/ov_repl.m2:708:0}, .}}}}

DIV{HEADER1{Down,  -- monomial ordering}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, TT{MonomialOrder},  -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic)., PARA{}, In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations., PARA{}, In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of , EM{ordering tests}, , of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: monomial orderings}, ., PARA{}, Permissible elements:, UL{LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GRevLex},  => n -- A graded reverse lexicographic block of variables}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Lex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Weights},  => {...}}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Position},  => Up  or  Position => Down}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: RevLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GroupLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GroupRevLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MonomialSize},  => n, n being 8,16,32, or 64.  Set the packing size for exponents for further variables}}, PARA{}, Some examples of monomial orders.  Note that if only one item is in the list, we can dispense with the list., UL{LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {GRevLex=>2, GRevLex=>3}},  -- a product order}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {2, 3}},  -- same}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {Weights=>{1,13,6,2}}},  -- a weight order}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => Weights=>{1,13,6,2}},  -- same}}, If any monomials will be less than 1 in the ordering, then the option , TT{Global => false},  should be used., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : QQ[x,y, Weights => {-1,1}, Global => false]

| runHooks(MutableHashTable, Thing, Thing) := true >> opts -> (store, key, args) -> (
|     store = if store#?key then store#key else (
|         if debugHooksLevel > 1 then printerr("runHooks: no hooks installed for ", toString key); return );
|     alg := if opts.?Strategy then opts.Strategy;
|     type := class alg;

|     -- if Strategy is given, and it is among the known strategies, run only that hook
|     if store.HookAlgorithms#?alg  then runHook(store.HookAlgorithms#alg,  key, alg,  args, opts) else

|     -- TODO: implement reverse lookup to find strategy installed under ancestors of type?
|     if store.HookAlgorithms#?type then runHook(store.HookAlgorithms#type, key, type, args, opts) else
|     -- otherwise, give an error with the list of possible strategies

For example, in Unix, it might be a named pipe.  A filename starting with , TT{~/},  will have the tilde replaced by the user's home directory.}, LI{a string of the form , TT{"!cmd"}, : the command , TT{cmd},  will be started, and two pipes will be opened, connected to its standard input and standard output file descriptors. Warning: pipes hold only 4096 bites, so if you write more than that to the resulting input output file (as input for the command) without reading any data, you may block while the command is blocked waiting to write more output; in this case, Macaulay2 will appear to hang.}, LI{a string of the form , TT{"$hostname:service"}, : a connection will be made to the specified service at the specified host.  If the service port is omitted, along with the colon, then port 2500 is used.  If the hostname is omitted, an incoming connection will be waited for.}, LI{a listener created previously by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: openListener}, : a new connection will be created.  To avoid blocking the Macaulay2 process while waiting for the incoming connection, use , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: isReady}, .}}, PARA{In order to open a socket successfully, there must be a process accepting connections for the desired service on the specified host.}, PARA{The various forms listed above can be used also with all other input output operations that open files, such as , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: openIn}, , , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: openOut}, , , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: get}, , and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: <<}, , with data transfer possible only in the direction specified.  A possibly confusing asymmetry is that with , TT{openIn "!foo"},  or with , TT{get "!foo"},  the standard input of the command , TT{foo},  is closed, but with , TT{openOut "!foo"},  the standard output of the command , TT{foo},  is connected to the standard output of the parent Macaulay2 process.}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: openIn}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: openOut}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: openListener}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{openInOut}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{openInOut(File)}}, LI{KBD{openInOut(String)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: openInOut},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: CompiledFunction, compiled function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/ov_system.m2:537:0}, .}}}}

See }, TO{Macaulay2Doc :: addHook}, TEX{ for where the hooks are stored.}}, PARA{TEX{Any other optional argument for }, TT{runHooks}, TEX{ that matches any key in }, TT{options hook}, TEX{ will be passed on to }, TT{hook}, TEX{. All other options are ignored.}}, PARA{TEX{For further explanation and examples of hooks see }, TO{Macaulay2Doc :: using hooks}, TEX{.}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, DIV{HEADER2{Code}, PRE{CODE{../../m2/option.m2:37:14-41:8: --source code:
  (opts,f) -> args -> (
       -- Common code for functions created with >> to separate options from arguments.
       -- uncurry(f, (new OptionTable from toList select(args, i -> instance(i,Option)), select(args, i -> not instance(i,Option))))
       uncurry(f, override (,args))
       )
| symbol  class            value                                                location of symbol
| ------  -----            -----                                                ------------------          
| f       FunctionClosure  FunctionClosure[../../m2/methods.m2:663:52-679:108]  ../../m2/option.m2:37:8-37:9
| opts    Boolean          true                                                 ../../m2/option.m2:37:3-37:7
| -- function f:
| ../../m2/methods.m2:663:52-679:108: --source code:
| runHooks(MutableHashTable, Thing, Thing) := true >> opts -> (store, key, args) -> (
|     store = if store#?key then store#key else (
|         if debugHooksLevel > 1 then printerr("runHooks: no hooks installed for ", toString key); return );
|     alg := if opts.?Strategy then opts.Strategy;
|     type := class alg;
|     -- if Strategy is not given, run through all available hooks
|     if alg === null then scan(reverse store.HookPriority, alg -> (
|             result := runHook(store.HookAlgorithms#alg, key, alg, args, opts ++ { Strategy => alg });
|             if not instance(result, Nothing) then break result)) else
|     -- if Strategy is given, and it is among the known strategies, run only that hook
|     if store.HookAlgorithms#?alg  then runHook(store.HookAlgorithms#alg,  key, alg,  args, opts) else
|     -- otherwise, if the class of alg is a known strategy, run only that hook
|     -- TODO: implement reverse lookup to find strategy installed under ancestors of type?
|     if store.HookAlgorithms#?type then runHook(store.HookAlgorithms#type, key, type, args, opts) else
|     -- otherwise, give an error with the list of possible strategies
|     error("unrecognized Strategy => '", toString alg, "' for ", toString key, newline,
|         "  available strategies are: ", demark_", " \\ toExternalString \ new List from store.HookPriority)), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: hooks}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: addHook}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{runHooks}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{runHooks(MutableHashTable,Thing,Thing)}}, LI{KBD{runHooks(Sequence,Thing)}}, LI{KBD{runHooks(Symbol,Thing)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: runHooks},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunctionWithOptions, method function with options}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/functions/hooks-doc.m2:181:0}, .}}}}

full_doc: DIV{HEADER1{run,  -- run an external command}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{run s, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{s}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: String, string}}, , , a command understandable by the operating system}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{SPAN{an , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: ZZ, integer}}, , , the return code}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, PARA{The process is run in the same process group, so signals invoked by control characters at the terminal will go both to it and to Macaulay2.}, PARA{Under Linux and Mac OS, the return code is 256 times the exit status code of the command, if the command exited normally; by convention, an exit status code of 0 indicates error free execution or the Boolean value , TT{true}, , an exit status code of 1 indicates an error or the Boolean value , TT{false}, ; if the command terminated in response to a signal or fault, the signal number (in the range 1-126) is returned, added to 128 if a core dump was created; if the shell (command interpreter) could not be executed, then 127 is returned. full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{irreducibleCharacteristicSeries,  -- irreducible characteristic series of an ideal}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{(ics,p) = irreducibleCharacteristicSeries I, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{I}, , , SPAN{an , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Ideal, ideal}}}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{ics}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: List, list}}, , , a list of matrices, representing an irreducible characteristic series for , TT{I}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{p}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: RingMap, ring map}}, , , an isomorphism from the ring of , TT{I},  to the ring of the characteristic series. The ring retains the names and degrees of the variables, but reorders the variables and uses a default monomial ordering.}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, PARA{TEX{ As we see in the example below, an irreducible characteristic series for $I$ consists of a collection of triangular sets. Here, given a polynomial $f$,  write $lvar(f)$ for the largest variable appearing in $f$ (with respect to the lexicographic order). In the example, $lvar(-y w+x^2) = y$ . A triangular set consists of polynomials $f_1,\dots,f_r$ such that $lvar(f_1)< \dots < lvar(f_r)$. In the example, $lvar(-x*y^2+z^3) = x < w = lvar(-w*y+z^2)$ . If $T_1,\dots,T_s$ form an irreducible characteristic series for $I$ , and if $J_i$ is the ideal generated by the largest variables of the elements of $T_i$ , then the algebraic set $V(I)$ defined by $I$ is the union of the sets $V(T_i) \setminus V(I_i)$, for $i=1,\dots,s$. The minimal associated primes of $I$ can thus be recovered from the irreducible characteristic series by saturation and by throwing away superfluous primes. }, This is done by , TO{MinimalPrimes :: minimalPrimes}, , which uses this routine.}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = QQ[w,x,y,z];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : (L,p) = irreducibleCharacteristicSeries ideal(x^2-y*w,x^3-z*w^2)

o2 = ({| zw2-x3 yw-x2 |, | x w |}, map (R, QQ[y..z, w..x], {y, z, w, x}))

o2 : Sequence, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : apply(L, m -> p m)

o3 = {| -x3+w2z -x2+wy |, | x w |}

o3 : List, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : p^-1

o4 = map (QQ[y..z, w..x], R, {w, x, y, z})

o4 : RingMap QQ[y..z, w..x] <-- R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{MinimalPrimes :: minimalPrimes}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{irreducibleCharacteristicSeries}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{irreducibleCharacteristicSeries(Ideal)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: irreducibleCharacteristicSeries},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/functions/irreducibleCharacteristicSeries-doc.m2:43:0}, .}}}}

name: Weights
full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{Weights,  -- assigning weights to the variables}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, Given a list L of n integers, the weight order on a polynomial ring in n variables is defined by: x^A > x^B if A_1 L_1 + ... + A_n L_n > B_1 L_1 + ... + B_n L_n., PARA{}, The leading component of a polynomial under a weight order need not be a monomial.  When two monomials have the same weight, by default they are further distinguished with the GRevLex order., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>{Weights => {-1,2,3,4}},Global=>false];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : f = a^2 + b+ c^2 + b*d

      2              2
o2 = c  + b*d + b + a

o2 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : leadTerm f

      2
o3 = c

o3 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, However, we can retrieve the entire leading component with the command , TT{leadTerm(1,f)}, . The plain , TT{leadTerm f},  is in this case the same as , TT{leadTerm(2,f)}, : they both use the full specification of the monomial ordering, first by weight and then by the , TT{GRevLex},  order.  In contrast, , TT{leadTerm(1,f)}, only distinguishes monomials by the first, i.e., weight, specification., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : leadTerm(1,ideal(f))

            2
o4 = ideal(c  + b*d)

o4 : Ideal of R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The weight order may be combined with further ordering elements to break ties. In the following example, we use a second weight vector to break ties under first weight vector., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : R = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>{Weights => {1,2,3,4}, Weights => {2,4,2,1}}];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : f = a^6 + b^3+ c^2

      6    3    2
o6 = a  + b  + c

o6 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : leadTerm(f)

      6
o7 = a

o7 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : leadTerm(1, ideal(f))

            6    3    2
o8 = ideal(a  + b  + c )

o8 : Ideal of R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : leadTerm(2, ideal(f))

            6    3
o9 = ideal(a  + b )

o9 : Ideal of R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : leadTerm(3, ideal(f))

             6
o10 = ideal a

o10 : Ideal of R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, TT{leadTerm(3, ideal(f))},  uses both the specified weights and the , TT{GRevLex},  order to calculate the leading component., PARA{}, When the number of weights is smaller than the number of variables, the remaining variables are given weight 0. In the following example, , TT{c},  and , TT{d},  have weight 0., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : R = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>{Weights => {1,2}, Lex}];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i12 : f = a^2 + b+ c^2 + b*d

       2              2
o12 = a  + b*d + b + c

o12 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: leadTerm}}}}, DIV{DIV{HEADER2{Functions with optional argument named , TT{Weights}, :}, UL{LI{SPAN{KBD{betti(...,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: betti(BettiTally)}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{minimalBetti(...,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: minimalBetti}}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: monoid(...,Weights=>...)}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{newRing(...,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: newRing}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{regularity(...,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: regularity}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{symmetricAlgebra(...,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: symmetricAlgebra}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{tensor(Monoid,Monoid,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: tensor(Monoid,Monoid)}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{tensor(Ring,Ring,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: tensor(Monoid,Monoid)}}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Weights},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Symbol, symbol}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/ov_monomial_orderings.m2:515:0}, .}}}}

The display includes the name of , TT{f}, , a sequence number in parentheses that tells how many times the function has been called, and a number in brackets that gives the nesting (recursion) depth. DIV{HEADER1{isWeylAlgebra, }, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, A Weyl algebra is the non-commutative algebra of algebraic differential operators on a polynomial ring.  To each variable , TT{x},  corresponds the operator , TT{dx},  that differentiates with respect to that variable.  The evident commutation relation takes the form , TT{dx*x == x*dx + 1}, ., PARA{}, We can give any names we like to the variables in a Weyl algebra, provided we specify the correspondence between the variables and the derivatives, with the , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: WeylAlgebra},  option, as follows., PARA{}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = QQ[x,y,dx,dy,t,WeylAlgebra => {x=>dx, y=>dy}]

o1 = R

o1 : PolynomialRing, 2 differential variable(s), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : dx*dy*x*y

o2 = x*y*dx*dy + x*dx + y*dy + 1

o2 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : dx*x^5

      5       4
o3 = x dx + 5x

o3 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, All modules over Weyl algebras are, in Macaulay2, right modules.  This means that multiplication of matrices is from the opposite side:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : dx*x

o4 = x*dx + 1

o4 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : matrix{{dx}} * matrix{{x}}

o5 = | xdx |

             1      1
o5 : Matrix R  <-- R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{All Gröbner basis and related computations work over this ring.  For an extensive collection of D-module routines (A D-module is a module over a Weyl algebra), see , TO{Dmodules :: Dmodules}, .}, PARA{The function , TT{isWeylAlgebra},  can be used to determine whether a polynomial ring has been constructed as a Weyl algebra.}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : isWeylAlgebra R

o6 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : S = QQ[x,y]

o7 = S

o7 : PolynomialRing, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : isWeylAlgebra S

o8 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{isWeylAlgebra}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{isWeylAlgebra(PolynomialRing)}}, LI{KBD{isWeylAlgebra(QuotientRing)}}, LI{KBD{isWeylAlgebra(Ring)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: isWeylAlgebra},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/ov_rings.m2:1347:0}, .}}}}

DIV{HEADER1{ParallelizeByDegree,  -- parallelism in engine computations}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, DIV{PARA{TEX{Some computations in the engine can run using multiple cores on your computer. Currently, this includes computation of minimal betti diagrams, non-minimal resolutions, and Gröbner bases of 2-sided ideals in associative algebras, all in the graded case, over a finite field.  Also included is (one of the algorithms for) the computation of Gröbner bases in polynomial rings over finite fields, whether graded or not.}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{The variable , TT{numTBBThreads},  controls the number of cores used by Macaulay2. The default value (zero) means the system can choose an appropriate number of cores (often the maximum available).  Note that the default behavior is to use multiple cores.}}, PARA{TEX{In }, TO{Macaulay2Doc :: minimalBetti}, TEX{, and in }, TO{Complexes :: freeResolution}, TEX{ with the , TT{Strategy => Nonminimal},  option, more aggressive parallelism that sometimes uses a lot of memory but can sometimes produce answers in less time can be enabled using the , TT{ParallelizeByDegree},  boolean option.}}, PARA{TEX{For examples, we show some simple examples of computation which, for larger size problems, might benefit from using parallelism.  Note that in each of these cases, the default is to use all available CPU cores for computation. full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{RRi,  -- the class of all real intervals}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, A real interval is entered as a pair of real numbers to the interval function.  It is stored internally as an arbitrary precision interval using the , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MPFI},  library., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : interval(3.1415,3.1416)

o1 = [3.1415,3.1416]

o1 : RRi (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The precision is measured in bits, is visible in the ring displayed on the second of each pair of output lines, and can be recovered using , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: precision}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : precision interval(3.1415,3.1416)

o2 = 53, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, For real intervals, the functions , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: class},  and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ring},  yield different results.  That allows numbers of various precisions to be used without creating a new ring for each precision., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : class interval(3.1,3.5)

o3 = RRi

o3 : InexactFieldFamily, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : ring interval(3.1,3.5)

o4 = RRi
        53

o4 : RealIntervalField, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The precision can be specified on input by specifying the precision of both input , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: RR},  numbers., Alternatively, the precision can be specified by including the option , TT{Precision}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : interval(2.5p100,3.2p1000)

o5 = [2.5,3.200000000000000000000000000001]

o5 : RRi (of precision 100), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : interval(2.5,3.2,Precision=>200)

o6 = [2.5,3.20000000000000017763568394002504646778106689453125]

o6 : RRi (of precision 200), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Intervals can also be created using , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: span(Sequence)},  to create the smallest interval containing the inputs., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : span(2,Precision=>100)

o7 = [2,2]

o7 : RRi (of precision 100), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : span(2,3,interval(-1.5,-0.5),73)

o8 = [-1.5,73]

o8 : RRi (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Operations using intervals are computed as sets so that the resulting intervals contain all possible outputs from pairs of points in input intervals., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : interval(1,3)+interval(2,4)

o9 = [3,7]

o9 : RRi (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : interval(-1,1)*interval(2,3)

o10 = [-3,3]

o10 : RRi (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : interval(0,1)-interval(0,1)

o11 = [-1,1]

o11 : RRi (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i12 : interval(1,2)/interval(1,2)

o12 = [.5,2]

o12 : RRi (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The notion of equality tested by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ==},  amounts to checking the equality of the endpoints of intervals., The notion of equality tested by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ===},  takes into account the precision of the inputs as well., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i13 : interval(1,3) == interval(1,3,Precision=>100)

o13 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i14 : interval(1,3) === interval(1,3,Precision=>100)

o14 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i15 : interval(1/3,1,Precision=>100)==interval(1/3,1,Precision=>1000)

o15 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The notion of inequalities for intervals amounts to testing the inequality for all points in the intervals.  In particular, , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: <=},  is not the same as , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: <},  or , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ==}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i16 : interval(1,2)<=interval(2,3)

o16 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i17 : interval(1,2)<=interval(1,2)

o17 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i18 : interval(1,2)<interval(2,3)

o18 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i19 : interval(1,2)<interval(3,4)

o19 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Transcendental functions on intervals produce intervals containing the image of the function on the interval., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i20 : exp(interval(2,4))

name: irreducibleCharacteristicSeries
full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{irreducibleCharacteristicSeries,  -- irreducible characteristic series of an ideal}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{(ics,p) = irreducibleCharacteristicSeries I, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{I}, , , SPAN{an , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Ideal, ideal}}}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{ics}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: List, list}}, , , a list of matrices, representing an irreducible characteristic series for , TT{I}}}, LI{SPAN{TT{p}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: RingMap, ring map}}, , , an isomorphism from the ring of , TT{I},  to the ring of the characteristic series. The ring retains the names and degrees of the variables, but reorders the variables and uses a default monomial ordering.}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, PARA{TEX{ As we see in the example below, an irreducible characteristic series for $I$ consists of a collection of triangular sets. Here, given a polynomial $f$,  write $lvar(f)$ for the largest variable appearing in $f$ (with respect to the lexicographic order). In the example, $lvar(-y w+x^2) = y$ . A triangular set consists of polynomials $f_1,\dots,f_r$ such that $lvar(f_1)< \dots < lvar(f_r)$. In the example, $lvar(-x*y^2+z^3) = x < w = lvar(-w*y+z^2)$ . If $T_1,\dots,T_s$ form an irreducible characteristic series for $I$ , and if $J_i$ is the ideal generated by the largest variables of the elements of $T_i$ , then the algebraic set $V(I)$ defined by $I$ is the union of the sets $V(T_i) \setminus V(I_i)$, for $i=1,\dots,s$. The minimal associated primes of $I$ can thus be recovered from the irreducible characteristic series by saturation and by throwing away superfluous primes. }, This is done by , TO{MinimalPrimes :: minimalPrimes}, , which uses this routine.}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = QQ[w,x,y,z];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : (L,p) = irreducibleCharacteristicSeries ideal(x^2-y*w,x^3-z*w^2)

o2 = ({| zw2-x3 yw-x2 |, | x w |}, map (R, QQ[y..z, w..x], {y, z, w, x}))

o2 : Sequence, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : apply(L, m -> p m)

o3 = {| -x3+w2z -x2+wy |, | x w |}

o3 : List, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : p^-1

o4 = map (QQ[y..z, w..x], R, {w, x, y, z})

o4 : RingMap QQ[y..z, w..x] <-- R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{MinimalPrimes :: minimalPrimes}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{irreducibleCharacteristicSeries}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{irreducibleCharacteristicSeries(Ideal)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: irreducibleCharacteristicSeries},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/functions/irreducibleCharacteristicSeries-doc.m2:43:0}, .}}}}

DIV{HEADER1{CC,  -- the class of all complex numbers}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, In Macaulay2, complex numbers are represented as floating point numbers, and so are only approximate.  The symbol , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ii},  represents the square root of -1 in many numeric contexts.  A complex number is obtained by using the symbolic constant , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ii},  or the conversion functions , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: toCC},  and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: numeric}, , in combination with real numbers (see , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: RR}, ). It is stored internally as a pair of arbitrary precision floating point real numbers, using the , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MPFR},  library., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : z = 3-4*ii

Weights
full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{Weights,  -- assigning weights to the variables}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, Given a list L of n integers, the weight order on a polynomial ring in n variables is defined by: x^A > x^B if A_1 L_1 + ... + A_n L_n > B_1 L_1 + ... + B_n L_n., PARA{}, The leading component of a polynomial under a weight order need not be a monomial.  When two monomials have the same weight, by default they are further distinguished with the GRevLex order., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>{Weights => {-1,2,3,4}},Global=>false];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : f = a^2 + b+ c^2 + b*d

      2              2
o2 = c  + b*d + b + a

o2 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : leadTerm f

      2
o3 = c

o3 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, However, we can retrieve the entire leading component with the command , TT{leadTerm(1,f)}, . The plain , TT{leadTerm f},  is in this case the same as , TT{leadTerm(2,f)}, : they both use the full specification of the monomial ordering, first by weight and then by the , TT{GRevLex},  order.  In contrast, , TT{leadTerm(1,f)}, only distinguishes monomials by the first, i.e., weight, specification., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : leadTerm(1,ideal(f))

            2
o4 = ideal(c  + b*d)

o4 : Ideal of R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The weight order may be combined with further ordering elements to break ties. In the following example, we use a second weight vector to break ties under first weight vector., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : R = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>{Weights => {1,2,3,4}, Weights => {2,4,2,1}}];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : f = a^6 + b^3+ c^2

      6    3    2
o6 = a  + b  + c

o6 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : leadTerm(f)

      6
o7 = a

o7 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : leadTerm(1, ideal(f))

            6    3    2
o8 = ideal(a  + b  + c )

o8 : Ideal of R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : leadTerm(2, ideal(f))

            6    3
o9 = ideal(a  + b )

o9 : Ideal of R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : leadTerm(3, ideal(f))

             6
o10 = ideal a

o10 : Ideal of R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, TT{leadTerm(3, ideal(f))},  uses both the specified weights and the , TT{GRevLex},  order to calculate the leading component., PARA{}, When the number of weights is smaller than the number of variables, the remaining variables are given weight 0. In the following example, , TT{c},  and , TT{d},  have weight 0., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : R = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>{Weights => {1,2}, Lex}];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i12 : f = a^2 + b+ c^2 + b*d

       2              2
o12 = a  + b*d + b + c

o12 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: leadTerm}}}}, DIV{DIV{HEADER2{Functions with optional argument named , TT{Weights}, :}, UL{LI{SPAN{KBD{betti(...,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: betti(BettiTally)}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{minimalBetti(...,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: minimalBetti}}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: monoid(...,Weights=>...)}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{newRing(...,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: newRing}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{regularity(...,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: regularity}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{symmetricAlgebra(...,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: symmetricAlgebra}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{tensor(Monoid,Monoid,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: tensor(Monoid,Monoid)}}}, LI{SPAN{KBD{tensor(Ring,Ring,Weights=>...)},  -- see , TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: tensor(Monoid,Monoid)}}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Weights},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Symbol, symbol}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/ov_monomial_orderings.m2:515:0}, .}}}}

name: setup
full_doc: DIV{HEADER1{setup, }, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{setup(), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{DIV{Consequences:, UL{LI{TEX{Initialization files for Emacs and the standard command shells will have lines added to them to allow the Macaulay2 files to be found. A missing initialization file will be created only if doing so will not prevent the command shell from reading further initialization files. The user is prompted before each file is modified and offered the opportunity to review or reject the changes.}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, DIV{PARA{TEX{Backup files are made carefully, and if a mangled initialization file is detected, it will not be modified. The lines added are bracketed by comment lines containing the phrases }, TT{Macaulay 2 start}, TEX{ and }, TT{Macaulay 2 end}, TEX{.}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{The initialization files will contain added commands that add the appropriate directory to the front of the environment variable }, TT{PATH}, TEX{ so the program }, TT{M2}, TEX{ can be found, unless that directory already occurs in the path, in which case it does not check whether that directory is the first one on the path containing a program whose name is }, TT{M2}, TEX{, for fear of escalating a competition with another init file.  (The expert user may prefer to remove those commands and instead, to create a symbolic link from a directory already on their path, such as }, TT{~/bin}, TEX{ or }, TT{~/.bin}, TEX{ to }, TT{M2}, TEX{.)}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{The other environment variables affected are }, TT{MANPATH}, TEX{, }, TT{INFOPATH}, TEX{, and }, TT{LD_LIBRARY_PATH}, TEX{.}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{This function is intended to be run only by users, not by system administrators, nor on behalf of users by system administrators, because system administrators can easily install Macaulay2 in such a way that the files can all be found.}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Caveat}, DIV{PARA{TEX{Warning: there is at least one important situation where you will not want to run the Macaulay2 }, TT{setup()}, TEX{ command. For example, suppose you have installed M2, not in its own private location as described above, but in a directory with many other executable files.  Suppose also that your account is adapted so it will run programs correctly on hardware of more than one architecture, or on differing operating systems, or even on various releases of the same operating system. Then }, TT{setup()}, TEX{ will modify your command shell init files so the directory containing M2 will be the first one searched when looking for a program. If you then try to use your account on different hardware, incorrect programs may be found, namely, those in the same directory as M2. Similarly, incorrect shareable libraries may also be found.}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: setupEmacs}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{setup}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{setup()}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: setup},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/functions/setup-doc.m2:68:0}, .}}}}

name: RR
full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{RR,  -- the class of all real numbers}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, A real number is entered as a sequence of decimal digits with a point.  It is stored internally as an arbitrary precision floating point number, using the , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MPFR},  library., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : 3.14159

o1 = 3.14159

o1 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The precision is measured in bits, is visible in the ring displayed on the second of each pair of output lines, and can be recovered using , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: precision}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : precision 3.14159

o2 = 53, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, For real numbers, the functions , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: class},  and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ring},  yield different results.  That allows numbers of various precisions to be used without creating a new ring for each precision., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : class 3.1

o3 = RR

o3 : InexactFieldFamily, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : ring 3.1

o4 = RR
       53

o4 : RealField, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The precision can be specified on input by appending the letter , TT{p},  and a positive number., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : 3p300

o5 = 3

o5 : RR (of precision 300), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, An optional exponent (for the power of ten to multiply by) can be specified on input by appending the letter , TT{e},  and a number., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : 3e3

o6 = 3000

o6 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : -3e-3

o7 = -.003

o7 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : -3p111e-3

o8 = -.003

o8 : RR (of precision 111), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Numbers that appear alone on an output line are displayed with all their meaningful digits. (Specifying 100 bits of precision yields about 30 decimal digits of precision.), TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : 1/3.

o9 = .3333333333333333

o9 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : 1/3p100

o10 = .3333333333333333333333333333335

o10 : RR (of precision 100), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : 100 * log(10,2)

o11 = 30.10299956639811

o11 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Numbers displayed inside more complicated objects are printed with the number of digits specified by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: printingPrecision}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i12 : printingPrecision

o12 = 6, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i13 : {1/3.,1/3p100}

o13 = {.333333, .333333}

o13 : List, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The notion of equality tested by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ==},  amounts to equality of the internal binary digits., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i14 : .5p100 == .5p30

o14 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i15 : .2p100 == .2p30

o15 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The notion of (strict) equality tested by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: ===},  also takes the precision into account., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i16 : .5p100 === .5p30

o16 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i17 : .2p100 === .2p30

o17 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Perhaps surprisingly, the IEEE floating point standard also specifies that every number, including 0, has a sign bit, and strict equality testing takes it into account, as it must do, because some arithmetic and transcendental functions take it into account., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i18 : 0.

o18 = 0

o18 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i19 : -0.

o19 = -0

o19 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i20 : 1/0.

o20 = infinity

o20 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i21 : 1/-0.

o21 = -infinity

o21 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i22 : log 0

o22 = -infinity

o22 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i23 : csc (0.)

o23 = infinity

o23 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i24 : csc (-0.)

o24 = -infinity

o24 : RR (of precision 53), class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, Use , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: toExternalString},  to produce something that, when encountered as input, will reproduce exactly what you had before., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i25 : x = {1/3.,1/3p100}

DIV{HEADER1{GRevLex,  -- graded reverse lexicographical monomial ordering}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, TEX{ The graded reverse lexicographic order is defined by: $x^A > x^B$ if either $degree(x^A) > degree(x^B)$ or $degree(x^A) = degree(x^B)$ and the LAST non-zero entry of the vector of integers $A-B$ is NEGATIVE. }, PARA{}, TEX{ This is the default order in Macaulay2, in large part because it is often the most efficient order for use with Gröbner bases.  By giving GRevLex a list of integers, one may change the definition of the order: $degree(x^A)$ is the dot product of $A$ with the argument of GRevLex.}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = QQ[a..d];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : a^3 + b^2 + b*c

            2    3
o4 = b*c + b  + a

o4 : S, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The largest possible exponent of variables in the , TT{GRevLex},  order is 2^31-1.  For efficiency reasons, it is sometimes useful to limit the size of monomials (this often makes computations more efficient)., Use , TT{MonomialSize => 16}, , which allows maximal exponent 2^15-1, or , TT{MonomialSize => 8}, , which allows maximal exponent 2^7-1., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : B1 = QQ[a..d,MonomialSize=>16,MonomialOrder=>GRevLex];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : B = QQ[a..d,MonomialSize=>16];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : a^(2^15-1)

o7 = a

name: isWeylAlgebra
full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{isWeylAlgebra, }, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, A Weyl algebra is the non-commutative algebra of algebraic differential operators on a polynomial ring.  To each variable , TT{x},  corresponds the operator , TT{dx},  that differentiates with respect to that variable.  The evident commutation relation takes the form , TT{dx*x == x*dx + 1}, ., PARA{}, We can give any names we like to the variables in a Weyl algebra, provided we specify the correspondence between the variables and the derivatives, with the , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: WeylAlgebra},  option, as follows., PARA{}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = QQ[x,y,dx,dy,t,WeylAlgebra => {x=>dx, y=>dy}]

o1 = R

o1 : PolynomialRing, 2 differential variable(s), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : dx*dy*x*y

o2 = x*y*dx*dy + x*dx + y*dy + 1

o2 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : dx*x^5

      5       4
o3 = x dx + 5x

o3 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, All modules over Weyl algebras are, in Macaulay2, right modules.  This means that multiplication of matrices is from the opposite side:, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : dx*x

o4 = x*dx + 1

o4 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : matrix{{dx}} * matrix{{x}}

o5 = | xdx |

             1      1
o5 : Matrix R  <-- R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, PARA{All Gröbner basis and related computations work over this ring.  For an extensive collection of D-module routines (A D-module is a module over a Weyl algebra), see , TO{Dmodules :: Dmodules}, .}, PARA{The function , TT{isWeylAlgebra},  can be used to determine whether a polynomial ring has been constructed as a Weyl algebra.}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : isWeylAlgebra R

o6 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : S = QQ[x,y]

o7 = S

o7 : PolynomialRing, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : isWeylAlgebra S

o8 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{isWeylAlgebra}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{isWeylAlgebra(PolynomialRing)}}, LI{KBD{isWeylAlgebra(QuotientRing)}}, LI{KBD{isWeylAlgebra(Ring)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: isWeylAlgebra},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/ov_rings.m2:1347:0}, .}}}}

name: OrderedMonoid
full_doc: DIV{HEADER1{OrderedMonoid,  -- the class of all ordered monoids}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, An ordered monoid is a multiplicative monoid together with an ordering of its elements.  The ordering is required to be compatible with the multiplication in the sense that if x < y then x z < y z.  The class of all ordered monoids is , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: OrderedMonoid}, ., PARA{}, The reason for making a separate class for ordered monoids is that monoid rings can be implemented more efficiently for them - an element of the monoid ring can be stored as a sorted list, each element of which is a pair consisting of an element of the monoid and a coefficient. See , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: PolynomialRing}, ., PARA{}, A free commutative ordered monoid can be created with , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: monoid}, .}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: Monoid}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Types of , ordered monoid, :}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: GeneralOrderedMonoid}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: OrderedMonoid},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Type, type}}, , with ancestor classes , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Monoid},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Type},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MutableHashTable},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: HashTable},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Thing}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/doc_rings.m2:34:0}, .}}}}

o2 : R, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, The largest possible exponent of variables in , TT{Lex},  order is 2^31-1.  For efficiency reasons, the size of the exponents of variables may be restricted.  Then instead of , TT{Lex}, , one can use , TT{ MonomialSize=>16}, , which allows maximal exponent 2^15-1, or , TT{MonomialSize=>8}, , which allows maximal exponent 2^7-1., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : B = QQ[a..d,MonomialOrder=>Lex,MonomialSize=>16];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : a^(2^15-1)

o4 = a

o6 = failed, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : a^(2^7-1)

name: Up
full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{Up,  -- monomial ordering}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, TT{MonomialOrder},  -- an optional argument used with polynomial rings and monoids to indicate a monomial ordering other than the default (graded reverse lexicographic)., PARA{}, In Macaulay2, each polynomial ring (and also each monoid) is equipped with a monomial order, which is used for display of polynomials (terms are listed in descending monomial order), and also for Gröbner basis computations., PARA{}, In the most general setting, a monomial ordering is given by a list of , EM{ordering tests}, , of various types listed and described below, each of which provides a partial ordering on the monomials.  The ordering tests are applied sequentially, starting with the first one, until one monomial is judged greater than the other. At the end, if necessary, the graded reverse lexicographic order is used to compare the monomials. For examples, see below, or see , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: monomial orderings}, ., PARA{}, Permissible elements:, UL{LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GRevLex},  => n -- A graded reverse lexicographic block of variables}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Lex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Weights},  => {...}}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Position},  => Up  or  Position => Down}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: RevLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GroupLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: GroupRevLex},  => n}, LI{TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MonomialSize},  => n, n being 8,16,32, or 64.  Set the packing size for exponents for further variables}}, PARA{}, Some examples of monomial orders.  Note that if only one item is in the list, we can dispense with the list., UL{LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {GRevLex=>2, GRevLex=>3}},  -- a product order}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {2, 3}},  -- same}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => {Weights=>{1,13,6,2}}},  -- a weight order}, LI{TT{MonomialOrder => Weights=>{1,13,6,2}},  -- same}}, If any monomials will be less than 1 in the ordering, then the option , TT{Global => false},  should be used., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : QQ[x,y, Weights => {-1,1}, Global => false]

o1 = QQ[x..y]

o1 : PolynomialRing, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : x<1

o2 = true, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : y<1

o3 = false, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: monomial orderings}}, LI{TOH{QthPower :: weightGrevlex}}, LI{TOH{QthPower :: grevlexWeight}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Up},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Symbol, symbol}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/ov_monomial_orderings.m2:704:0}, .}}}}

full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{fold,  -- apply a binary operator repeatedly}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{fold(f, x, L), class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{fold(f, L), class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{fold(L, x, f), class => language-macaulay2}}, DD{CODE{fold(L, f), class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{f}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Function, function}}, , }}, LI{SPAN{TT{x}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Thing, thing}}, , }}, LI{SPAN{TT{L}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: VisibleList, visible list}}, , , TEX{or an instance of a class with the }, TO{Macaulay2Doc :: iterator}, TEX{ method installed}}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{M}, , , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: List, list}}, , }}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, DIV{PARA{TEX{Suppose , TT{L=\{x0, x1, ..., xn\}}, . Then for any binary operator , TT{f}, , , TT{fold(f, L)},  computes , TT{f(...f(f(x0, x1), x2), ...)}, . In other words, the binary operator is applied to the first two elements of , TT{L}, , then to that result along with the next unused element of , TT{L}, , and so forth.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : fold(plus, {0,1,2,3,4,5})

o1 = 15, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : fold(identity, {a,b,c,d,e})

o2 = ((((a, b), c), d), e)

o2 : Sequence, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i3 : fold((i,j) -> i|j|i, {"a","b","c","d","e"})

o3 = abacabadabacabaeabacabadabacaba, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{If , TT{fold(f, x, L)},  is called, the element , TT{x},  is used as the first argument of the binary function , TT{f}, . In other words, , TT{fold(f, \{x0, x1, \ldots, xn\})},  is equivalent to , TT{fold(f, x0, \{x1, \ldots, xn\})}, .}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i4 : fold(plus, 0, {1,2,3,4,5})

o4 = 15, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i5 : fold((x, y) -> x^y, 2, {3,2,1,2})

o5 = 4096, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{The function , TT{fold(\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n\}, f)},  returns , TT{f...f(f(x_{n-2}, f(x_{n-1}, x_n)))}, . That is, , TT{f},  is applied to the last two elements of the list first, then the repeated calls to , TT{f},  proceed backwards through the list. The optional argument , TT{x},  in , TT{fold(L, x, f)},  is used as the second argument in the first evaluation of , TT{f}, . So , TT{fold(\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_{n-1}\}, x_n, f)},  is equivalent to , TT{fold(\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_n\}, f)}, .}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i6 : fold({a,b,c,d,e}, identity)

o6 = (a, (b, (c, (d, e))))

o6 : Sequence, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i7 : fold({a,b,c,d}, e, identity)

o7 = (a, (b, (c, (d, e))))

o7 : Sequence, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i8 : fold({2,3,2,1}, 2, (x, y) -> x^y)

o8 = 512, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{If }, TT{L}, TEX{ is an instance of class the the }, TO{Macaulay2Doc :: iterator}, TEX{ method installed, e.g., a string, then it may also be used with }, TT{fold}, TEX{, but only the versions with }, TT{f}, TEX{ as the first argument.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i9 : fold(identity, "abcde")

o9 = ((((a, b), c), d), e)

o9 : Sequence, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i10 : fold(identity, "a", "bcde")

o10 = ((((a, b), c), d), e)

o10 : Sequence, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}, DIV{PARA{TEX{The difference between }, TO{Macaulay2Doc :: fold}, TEX{ and , TT{accumulate},  is that , TT{fold},  returns the final result of all the nested evaluations of , TT{f}, , while , TT{accumulate},  lists all the intermediate values as well.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i11 : accumulate({2,3,2,1}, 2, (x, y) -> x^y)

o11 = {512, 9, 2, 1}

o11 : List, class => language-macaulay2}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: apply}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: accumulate}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: lists and sequences}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{fold}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{fold(Function,Thing)}}, LI{KBD{fold(Function,Thing,Thing)}}, LI{KBD{fold(Function,VisibleList)}}, LI{KBD{fold(VisibleList,Function)}}, LI{KBD{fold(VisibleList,Thing,Function)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: fold},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: MethodFunction, method function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/functions/fold-doc.m2:74:0}, .}}}}

For example, in Unix, it might be a named pipe.  A filename starting with , TT{~/},  will have the tilde replaced by the user's home directory.}, LI{a string of the form , TT{"!cmd"}, : the command , TT{cmd},  will be started, and two pipes will be opened, connected to its standard input and standard output file descriptors. Warning: pipes hold only 4096 bites, so if you write more than that to the resulting input output file (as input for the command) without reading any data, you may block while the command is blocked waiting to write more output; in this case, Macaulay2 will appear to hang.}, LI{a string of the form , TT{"$hostname:service"}, : a connection will be made to the specified service at the specified host.  If the service port is omitted, along with the colon, then port 2500 is used.  If the hostname is omitted, an incoming connection will be waited for.}, LI{a listener created previously by , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: openListener}, : a new connection will be created.  To avoid blocking the Macaulay2 process while waiting for the incoming connection, use , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: isReady}, .}}, PARA{In order to open a socket successfully, there must be a process accepting connections for the desired service on the specified host.}, PARA{The various forms listed above can be used also with all other input output operations that open files, such as , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: openIn}, , , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: openOut}, , , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: get}, , and , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: <<}, , with data transfer possible only in the direction specified.  A possibly confusing asymmetry is that with , TT{openIn "!foo"},  or with , TT{get "!foo"},  the standard input of the command , TT{foo},  is closed, but with , TT{openOut "!foo"},  the standard output of the command , TT{foo},  is connected to the standard output of the parent Macaulay2 process.}}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: openIn}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: openOut}}, LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: openListener}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Ways to use , TT{openInOut}, :}, UL{LI{KBD{openInOut(File)}}, LI{KBD{openInOut(String)}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: openInOut},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: CompiledFunction, compiled function}}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/ov_system.m2:537:0}, .}}}}

full_doc:
DIV{HEADER1{randomKRationalPoint,  -- pick a random K rational point on the scheme X defined by I}, UL{LI{DL{class => element, DT{Usage: }, DD{CODE{randomKRationalPoint I, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, LI{Inputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{TT{I}, , , SPAN{an , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Ideal, ideal}}, , , TEX{in a polynomial ring over a finite ground field K}}}}}, LI{Outputs:, UL{LI{SPAN{SPAN{an , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Ideal, ideal}}, , , TEX{of a K-rational point on V(I)}}}}}}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, DIV{PARA{TEX{If X has codimension 1, then we intersect X with a randomly chosen line, and hope that the decomposition of the intersection contains a K-rational point. If n=degree X then the probability P that this happens, is the proportion  of permutations in $S_n$ with a fix point on $\{1,\ldots,n \}$, i.e. $$P=\sum_{j=1}^n (-1)^{j-1} binomial(n,j)(n-j)!/n! = 1-1/2+1/3! + \ldots $$ which approaches $1-exp(-1) = 0.63\ldots$. Thus a probabilistic approach works.}}, PARA{TEX{For higher codimension we first project X birationally onto a hypersurface Y, and find a point on Y. Then we take the preimage of this point.}}}, TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : p=nextPrime(random(2*10^4))

name: OrderedMonoid
full_doc: DIV{HEADER1{OrderedMonoid,  -- the class of all ordered monoids}, DIV{HEADER2{Description}, An ordered monoid is a multiplicative monoid together with an ordering of its elements.  The ordering is required to be compatible with the multiplication in the sense that if x < y then x z < y z.  The class of all ordered monoids is , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: OrderedMonoid}, ., PARA{}, The reason for making a separate class for ordered monoids is that monoid rings can be implemented more efficiently for them - an element of the monoid ring can be stored as a sorted list, each element of which is a pair consisting of an element of the monoid and a coefficient. See , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: PolynomialRing}, ., PARA{}, A free commutative ordered monoid can be created with , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: monoid}, .}, DIV{HEADER2{See also}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: Monoid}}}}, DIV{DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{Types of , ordered monoid, :}, UL{LI{TOH{Macaulay2Doc :: GeneralOrderedMonoid}}}}, DIV{class => waystouse, HEADER2{For the programmer}, PARA{The object , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: OrderedMonoid},  is , SPAN{a , TO2{Macaulay2Doc :: Type, type}}, , with ancestor classes , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Monoid},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Type},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: MutableHashTable},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: HashTable},  < , TO{Macaulay2Doc :: Thing}, .}}, HR{}, DIV{class => waystouse, PARA{The source of this document is in , TT{Macaulay2Doc/doc_rings.m2:34:0}, .}}}}

Thus a probabilistic approach works.}}, PARA{TEX{For higher codimension we first project X birationally onto a hypersurface Y, and find a point on Y. The pseudo remainder of , TT{f},  by , TT{g},  is the polynomial , TT{h},  of degree less than , TT{d},  in , TT{x},  such that , TT{c^(e-d+1) * f = q*g + h}, , where , TT{f},  has degree , TT{e},  in , TT{x}, ., TABLE{class => examples, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i1 : R = QQ[x,y];, class => language-macaulay2}}}}, TR{TD{PRE{CODE{i2 : f = x^4
